title: Where does a computer put apple?
hook: Sort apple, Banana and Zebra by the numbers a computer stores. Where does each land?

doesNotKnow: that each character is stored as a number code
that every capital letter's code is smaller than every small letter's, so sorting by the stored numbers is not dictionary order

misconception: A computer stores letters as letters, so when it sorts words it puts them in dictionary order.
objective: The learner can say that each letter is stored as a number (A 65 to Z 90, a 97 to z 122), so sorting by code puts every capitalised word before every lowercase one (Banana, Zebra, apple), and that ignoring case or language-aware rules give dictionary order.

claims.text: In ASCII, and in Unicode's first 128 code points, A is 65, B 66, Z 90, a 97, z 122 (stage ruler 'A 65 … Z 90 · a 97 … z 122'; tile codes Z = 90, a = 97, B = 66).
claims.source: Builder re-ran in node 2026-10-14: 'A'.charCodeAt(0) = 65, B 66, Z 90, a 97, b 98, z 122. RFC 20 (ASCII format for network interchange, 1969) code table; Unicode Standard, Basic Latin chart U+0000-U+007F. Demo.tsx computes every code with charCodeAt. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node charCodeAt and Buffer 'ascii' encoding: A 65, B 66, Z 90, a 97, b 98, z 122. Python 3 unicodedata (UCD 15.1.0, shipped with the interpreter): U+0041 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A … U+007A LATIN SMALL LETTER Z at the same values, and Python's ascii codec gives the same bytes. RFC 20 and the Unicode chart not opened (hosts blocked); the encodings that ship with node and Python are the openable artifacts. Stage RULER is built with charCodeAt: 'A 65 … Z 90 · a 97 … z 122'; tiles show 'Z = 90', 'a = 97', 'B = 66'.

claims.text: Sorting Zebra, apple, Banana by character code gives Banana, Zebra, apple, so Banana and Zebra come ahead of apple.
claims.source: Node 2026-10-14: ['Zebra','apple','Banana'].sort() = [Banana, Zebra, apple] (default sort compares UTF-16 code units, ECMA-262 Array.prototype.sort). Demo.tsx uses the same code-unit comparison. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: ['Zebra','apple','Banana'].sort() = Banana, Zebra, apple; Demo byCode compares strings with < (UTF-16 code units). Reveal 'put Banana and Zebra ahead of apple' is computed from CODE_ORDER. Predict answer index 2 = 'Last' matches.

claims.text: Ignoring case (comparing lowercased letters) gives apple, Banana, Zebra, so apple comes first.
claims.source: Node 2026-10-14: sorting on toLowerCase() keys gives [apple, Banana, Zebra]. Demo.tsx byLower. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: sorting on toLowerCase() gives apple, Banana, Zebra; reveal prints CASE_ORDER[0] = apple; reveal needs milestone case-ignored.

claims.text: Each small letter's code is its capital's code plus 32.
claims.source: Node loop over A-Z 2026-10-14: lowercase code minus capital code = 32 for all 26 letters (32 = 2^5, one bit). Demo.tsx computes GAP = 'a' - 'A'. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node over all 26 letters: small minus capital = 32 and toLowerCase maps each capital to that code; Python unicodedata names pair CAPITAL/SMALL for each. Reveal prints GAP = 32.

claims.text: To list words for people, a program can sort with language rules (collation) instead of raw codes, and those rules put apple first (apple, Banana, Zebra).
claims.source: Unicode Technical Standard #10 (Unicode Collation Algorithm); node 2026-10-14: ['Zebra','apple','Banana'].sort(new Intl.Collator('en').compare) = [apple, Banana, Zebra]. Wording is general ('real apps'); the fact-checker should judge whether 'usually' is needed. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. As worded the sentence is false: real software commonly sorts text by raw codes. Openable evidence on this host: GNU sort with LC_ALL=C (and C.UTF-8) prints Banana Zebra apple; Python sorted() gives ['Banana','Zebra','apple']; JavaScript's default Array.prototype.sort() does the same, as this lesson's own c2 shows. node Intl.Collator('en') (ICU 77.1) gives apple, Banana, Zebra, so language-aware collation exists, but 'real apps sort … not raw codes' overstates it. UTS #10 not opened. Fix (builder; owner decides wording): qualify the claim, e.g. say that apps sorting words for people usually use language rules (collation) rather than raw codes, and give a source that can be opened. Blocks publishing. | Builder fix v2 (2026-10-14, W-497): reworded from 'Real apps sort text with language rules, not raw codes', which FC pass 35 found false as a general statement (GNU sort LC_ALL=C, Python sorted() and JS default sort order by code). New wording claims only that language-aware sorting exists and gives this order. Openable evidence on this host: node 2026-10-14 (ICU 77.1): ['Zebra','apple','Banana'].sort(new Intl.Collator('en').compare) and .sort((a,b)=>a.localeCompare(b)) both give [apple, Banana, Zebra]. Intl.Collator is specified by ECMA-402 (ECMAScript Internationalization API), section 10 Collator Objects; ICU implements the Unicode Collation Algorithm (UTS #10). Specs not opened from this host. Needs a fresh fact-check. | FC pass 36 (fact-checker, fresh instance, 2026-10-14, W-637): VERIFIED (v2). Own node v22.22.0 (ICU 77.1): ['Zebra','apple','Banana'].sort(new Intl.Collator(loc).compare) and localeCompare give apple, Banana, Zebra for en, en-US, en-GB, de, fr, sv and the default locale, while the default sort() gives Banana, Zebra, apple (Demo byCode). The claim now asserts only that language-rule sorting exists and gives this order; a running collator on this host demonstrates both. Reveal 'a program can sort with language rules instead, which put apple first' matches. ECMA-402 and UTS #10 not opened (tc39.es DNS failure); not relied on.

claims.text: A computer stores each letter as a number, and every capital (65 to 90) comes before every small letter (97 to 122).
claims.source: Follows from c1: the capital range 65-90 ends below the small-letter range 97-122. Character encodings (ASCII, Unicode) assign each character a number; RFC 20; Unicode Standard ch. 2. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Follows from c1 (verified): every capital 65-90 is below every small letter 97-122. Reveal prints the ranges from charCodeAt. 'Stores each letter as a number' is true of these encodings (node and Python encode each letter as one byte/code unit).

recall.question: A program sorts the words cat and Dog by their stored letter codes. Which comes first?
recall.why: Capitals have smaller codes than small letters (D is 68, c is 99), so Dog sorts before cat by code, even though c comes before d in the alphabet.
